event.centerRule: Jesus remains the central person of the Event. Each tomb witness, appearance, meal, commission, proclamation, and later reuse remains attached to its own Scripture source rather than being merged into a synthetic harmony.

characterAnchors.label: Jesus
characterAnchors.note: Predicts rising, is announced as risen, appears, speaks peace, shows wounds, eats, interprets Scripture, commissions witnesses, and is named in later proclamation.

characterAnchors.label: Mary Magdalene
characterAnchors.note: Comes to the tomb in all four Gospel witness traditions and receives or carries resurrection testimony.

characterAnchors.label: Women witnesses
characterAnchors.note: Bring spices, inspect the tomb, encounter messengers, remember, fear, rejoice, flee, worship, and report in distinct accounts.

characterAnchors.label: Peter
characterAnchors.note: Runs to inspect the tomb, appears in later encounters, and publicly proclaims the raised Jesus.

characterAnchors.label: The beloved disciple
characterAnchors.note: Runs with Peter, inspects the linen, appears by the sea, and is associated with written testimony.

characterAnchors.label: Thomas
characterAnchors.note: Moves from rejecting the disciples’ report to encountering Jesus and confessing in the gathered room.

characterAnchors.label: Two travelers
characterAnchors.note: Recount the recent events, hear Scripture interpreted, recognize Jesus in bread, and return to Jerusalem.

characterAnchors.label: The eleven
characterAnchors.note: Receive reports, appearances, bodily evidence, interpretation, commissions, promised power, and the visible departure.

characterAnchors.label: Paul
characterAnchors.note: Encounters the risen Jesus near Damascus, retells that encounter before changing audiences, proclaims resurrection, and preserves received testimony and later reasoning in the letters.

event.throughline: Earlier sources name awakening and life beyond death; Jesus predicts rising; women and disciples encounter an empty tomb and the risen Jesus through distinct Gospel sequences; Acts preserves post-ascension sight, address, and public witness; the letters and Revelation then trace raised life, bodily hope, firstborn language, and death’s final horizon.

topic.orientation: Enter the Resurrection through earlier Jewish hope and four distinct Gospel witnesses, then inspect recognition, meals, commissions, post-ascension encounters, public proclamation, bodily hope, and later Scripture memory. The sources remain connected without being merged into one unreported chronology.
